cim: A look at VC-backed glossy magazine Colossus, whose glowing profiles of Zuckerberg and other tech titans win industry praise, as Kara Swisher says it is PR (Andrew Fedorov/The San Francisco Standard)
cim_eredeti: A look at VC-backed glossy magazine Colossus, whose glowing profiles of Zuckerberg and other tech titans win industry praise, as Kara Swisher says it is PR (Andrew Fedorov/The San Francisco Standard)
szoveg_eredeti:
A venture capitalist’s glossy quarterly wants to be The New Yorker for tech billionaires.

Inside tech’s corner offices, there’s no love left for the news media. “I think you’re the problem, the media,” Elon Musk told The Economist’s editor, Zanny Minton Beddoes, in July (opens in new tab). “You are loathed far more than I am.”

Colossus (opens in new tab), a lushly produced, oversize print quarterly and website, wants to make tech fall in love again. Launched in 2024, its journalistic approach — heavy on access, short on skepticism — has been heaped with praise by the very entrepreneurs and investors it covers.

“Gives me hope for journalism,” Reddit cofounder and venture capitalist Alexis Ohanian wrote (opens in new tab) on X. “This is by far the best profile I have ever read on a firm,” hedge fund manager Bill Ackman posted (opens in new tab) about a cover story (opens in new tab) on Thrive Capital founder Joshua Kushner. LinkedIn cofounder and venture capitalist Reid Hoffman shared (opens in new tab) the Kushner profile, writing, “Highly recommend giving this a read.”

Indeed, tech investors like Kushner are opening their homes and clearing their calendars for Colossus, while remaining largely inaccessible to mainstream media. The magazine has featured lengthy, gauzy cover stories on Greenoaks Capital’s Neil Mehta, Conviction’s Sarah Guo, Hyperliquid’s Jeff Yan, and Trilogy Software’s Joe Liemandt. In September, Colossus scored its biggest get yet, publishing a 15,000-word cover story (opens in new tab) on Mark Zuckerberg that featured scenes with the Meta CEO and his family at their various homes. “It’s the single best profile I have ever read of anyone,” one reader posted (opens in new tab).

Journalists, on the other hand, are unimpressed. “It is PR,” said veteran tech reporter Kara Swisher, who famously made Zuckerberg sweat (opens in new tab). “These people are so fragile and made of papier-mâché that they need Vaseline mirrors to reflect them back at themselves.”

“I think Kara is wrong when she calls it just PR,” countered Hiten Samtani, who runs a commercial real estate-focused media company and has written favorably about Colossus (opens in new tab). “If it were just PR, it would be much easier to ignore.”

Many media veterans doubt the profiles accomplish their subjects’ public relations goals. “It’s all well and good for the tech industry media bubble to have its own in-flight magazine, but audiences aren’t stupid,” Nilay Patel, editor-in-chief of The Verge, said in an email. “Writing a massive profile of Mark Zuckerberg in which … his staggering unpopularity with everyday Americans is treated as an unfortunate byproduct of his ambition just isn’t going to convince anyone of anything.

“If Mark actually wanted to be understood as he says he does, he’d sit down for a truly adversarial journalistic interview and try to make his case,” Patel added. “But I don’t think he can take the risk.”

Colossus is the brainchild of Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a Connecticut-raised heir to an oil fortune, who went to work for his father James’ firm, O’Shaughnessy Asset Management, in 2007. Patrick took over the company in 2018 and sold it four years later to Franklin Templeton. In 2016, he launched a podcast called “Invest Like the Best,” borrowing the title of a book his father published in 1994.

His guests on the podcast have included Berkshire Hathaway Vice Chairman Charlie Munger and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. In 2020, building on the success of “Invest Like the Best,” which O’Shaughnessy has said gets north of 100,000 downloads per episode, he launched a podcast network called Colossus, which now has shows like “Business Breakdowns” and “Founders.” The same year, he spun up a venture capital firm, Positive Sum.

When O’Shaughnessy started thinking about adding a print magazine to the Colossus stable, he recruited Jeremy Stern to serve as editor-in-chief and write its most prominent profiles, including those of Kushner and Zuckerberg. Stern had been deputy editor of Tablet, where he wrote a widely praised, if deeply sympathetic, profile (opens in new tab) of Anduril founder Palmer Luckey. Officially, Colossus appears to be a side project of Positive Sum, with many on its masthead listed (opens in new tab) as part of the firm’s team. Neither O’Shaughnessy nor Stern responded to requests for comment.

O’Shaughnessy was not the first VC or tech company to realize the value of a publication for those disillusioned with traditional journalism. Believing the tech press was untrustworthy and superficial, Andreessen Horowitz launched Future.com (opens in new tab) in 2021, then shut it down the next year. Stripe started publishing its quarterly magazine Increment in 2017, running for 19 issues; it now publishes books through Stripe Press and a magazine and website called Works in Progress (opens in new tab). In April, OpenAI acquired “TBPN,” a talk show made exclusively for and by tech bros.

Occasionally, these sorts of media ventures backfire in hilarious ways. In September 2022, weeks before FTX collapsed, Sequoia Capital self-published a glowing profile (opens in new tab) of Sam Bankman-Fried. “I couldn’t shake the feeling that this guy is actually as selfless as he claims to be,” its writer declared.

“It’s actually great that venture capitalists are now writing all of the founder hagiography, because it means that when, inevitably, one of these people goes to prison, the blowback will not affect mainstream journalists,” said Casey Newton, founder of Platformer and cohost of the new NPR podcast, “Machine Gods.” “It will just affect the venture class, and they can take it.”

But Colossus is the first in this wave of VC-sponsored media to make a serious effort to ape the writing and photography of glossy magazines. “This kind of wet kiss has always existed, but it was never done this artfully,” said Samtani. “To be super clear, it is not journalism. It is positioned, oftentimes, as journalism. They hire journalists, but it is not journalism. Think of it as high-grade, tier-one content marketing.”

If Colossus is content marketing, who is it marketing to? Annual subscriptions run $299, which works out to $74.75 per issue. (Back issues are a relative steal at $50 a piece (opens in new tab).) Even tech publicists are confused. “Who actually subscribes to it other than the other investors and entrepreneurs also seeking their own editorial platforms?” asked Brooke Hammerling, founder of the communications advisory firm The New New Thing.

The upside is less for the magazine itself, Samtani explained, than for O’Shaughnessy’s venture firm. “Their economics are not media company economics. This is at least partly a clout exercise and an access game, and it’s a very smart one,” he said. “Media is an incredible way to create connections and develop your own influence.”

Still, the people behind Colossus try to position the magazine within the traditions of legitimate journalism. On his colleague David Senra’s eponymous podcast (opens in new tab), distributed by the Colossus network, O’Shaughnessy paraphrased New Yorker editor David Remnick’s introduction to a compilation of the magazine’s profiles, saying the best examples “are defined by somebody doing a thing they’re obsessed with and a writer that is as obsessed with the person as the person is with the thing.” It was an aha moment for O’Shaughnessy: “Wow, that’s what I want to read.”

Notably, O’Shaughnessy failed to absorb the first paragraph of Remnick’s introduction, which establishes the form’s ethos. He wrote that The New Yorker’s founding editor, Harold Ross, “prized intimacy and wit over biographical completeness or, God forbid, unabashed hero worship. Ross told his writers and editors that, above all, he wanted to get away from what he was reading in the other magazines — all the ‘Horatio Alger’ stuff.”
